problem: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some nights; the cron entry and the backup script have not changed in months.

root: The job runs from a classic cron daemon on a single host, not a scheduler that replays missed runs.
The script guards against overlap with a lock file and exits quietly when the lock is held.
Cron has no MAILTO set and script output is not captured, so failures leave no trace.
1: The backup runs on a Linux host using a classic cron daemon (cronie or Vixie cron) from a user or /etc/crontab entry.
The backup is scheduled in the early morning, overlapping common patch-reboot and provider maintenance windows.
The host applies OS updates automatically (for example unattended-upgrades) and may reboot itself afterwards.
The host is a virtual machine whose power state can be affected by idle policies or a cloud provider.
2: The script guards against overlap with a plain lock file checked at startup, not flock or a systemd unit.
The dump uses a CLI tool such as pg_dump or mysqldump, then uploads the file to remote or network storage.
Cron output from the job is discarded or unmailed, and monitoring looks only at the job's exit status.
3: The cron entry schedules the backup at a minute between 02:00 and 03:00 local time, such as 02:30.
The host clock observes daylight saving time, so the skipped nights are spring-forward transitions.
The backup runs under busybox crond in a minimal container image, set up more than a few months ago, which does not replay skipped wall-clock minutes.
Staging hosts run in UTC while production uses the local zone.

reading: Top-level whys answer 'Why does the problem occur?'. Each node's whys answer 'Why <that node's reason>?'. An id is the dotted path from the top, so 2.4.1 is the 1st reason under 2.4, which is the 4th reason under 2. index.md lists the top 1 level(s) and the Read windows for this file; hygiene.json holds mechanical flags only.

whys.reason: The host is rebooted or suspended during the scheduled window, and cron never replays a run it missed.
Automatic OS updates are configured to reboot the host at a fixed early-morning time overlapping the backup's cron minute.
The auto-reboot time was left at the distro default and never compared against the backup entry in the crontab.
Patching and backups are owned by different people, with no shared schedule listing both jobs' times.
Kernel updates require a restart because no live-patching was adopted, so auto-reboot was enabled as the default fix.
The backup is scheduled through plain cron instead of anacron or a systemd timer with Persistent=true.
The crontab entry was copied from an older always-on server where the host was never down at night.
Anacron only catches up jobs in /etc/cron.daily, and nobody realised a user crontab entry gets no catch-up.
Migrating to a systemd timer would change the script's environment and logging, so the working entry was left alone.
The VM is suspended or powered off overnight by policies outside the backup job's control.
An idle power policy suspends the VM when no sessions are active, and the backup takes no sleep inhibitor lock.
The cloud provider schedules host maintenance and live-migration pauses in early-morning hours matching the backup time.
A cost-saving auto-stop schedule was added to shut down low-traffic VMs overnight without checking scheduled jobs.
A slow prior run or stale lock file makes the script exit early without dumping the database.
The lock file is removed only on a normal exit, so a killed or crashed run leaves it behind.
Cleanup relies on a shell trap on EXIT, which never fires when the OOM killer or SIGKILL ends the process.
The lock file sits in the backup directory on persistent disk rather than tmpfs, so it outlives the dead process.
The lock records no PID or start time, so the script cannot tell a dead holder from a live one.
The lock-found branch exits with status zero and no alert, so a skipped night looks like success.
The skip message goes to stdout, which the crontab redirects to /dev/null with no MAILTO set.
Monitoring checks only the cron job's exit code, not the age of the newest backup file.
The skip path was written for rare overlaps and never tested, so nobody reviewed how it reports itself.
The dump and upload steps have no timeout, so a stalled run keeps holding the lock into the next night.
The dump tool waits indefinitely for table locks held by long transactions or overnight maintenance jobs.
Uploads to the network storage mount block forever when the mount stalls, since no transfer timeout is configured.
The database has grown for months while the unchanged script still dumps uncompressed in one pass, lengthening every run.
The cron time falls in the daylight-saving changeover hour, so that night's scheduled minute never occurs.
The backup minute was set to 02:30 local time, inside the hour that clocks skip each spring.
The window was picked from a load graph showing lowest database traffic at 02:00-03:00, ignoring calendar clock shifts.
The crontab line was copied from an older UTC server, where 02:30 never collided with a clock change.
Crontab changes are reviewed without any rule flagging schedules between 01:00 and 03:00 local as DST-sensitive.
Cron evaluates the schedule in the host's DST-observing local timezone instead of UTC.
The server image sets the office's local zone so log timestamps match what on-call engineers read.
Provisioning accepted the installer's regional timezone default, and configuration management never enforces UTC on database hosts.
The crontab has no CRON_TZ=UTC line, so the backup entry silently inherits the system zone.
The cron daemon running the job has no catch-up logic for wall-clock minutes skipped by a DST jump.
The backup moved into a minimal Alpine container, which ships busybox crond rather than cronie with DST compensation.
Busybox crond documentation never mentions DST behaviour, so the gap was invisible when the image was chosen.
Staging runs in UTC, so no DST transition was ever exercised before the schedule reached production.
